prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification of topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: B041 remains my first choice. Band topology combined with spin-orbit coupling gave a new classification of insulators, and the discovery is at the centre: the quantum spin Hall edge channels were measured in HgTe wells and the concept has since been confirmed across many materials by transport, ARPES and scanning probes. Fifteen to twenty years of independent confirmation, a stable interpretation, and a reach well beyond solids make this overdue rather than premature. I have changed my preferred configuration. In round 1 I named Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan. After the full exchange I now prefer Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The Kane-Mele Z2 paper is a single joint theoretical contribution, and a configuration that separates its authors is harder to defend than one that follows the causal chain from prediction to first observation. Five of my colleagues arrived at this set independently, but I move because of the attribution argument, not because of the count.
statement.case_against: The credit is still incomplete whichever trio is chosen. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state that Molenkamp measured, and Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy are central to the three-dimensional theory; none can be named under the three-person limit. Hasan's ARPES demonstration of three-dimensional topological insulators is a major experimental result that this configuration leaves out, so a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect risks looking narrow. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions covers part of the conceptual background, and the committee should be explicit about what is new here: protected edge and surface states in real materials, and the Z2 classification with time-reversal symmetry. Finally, optical lattice clocks (B013) have the tidiest attribution on the shortlist, and a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize leaves them for a later year.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B029 to B041 because the Kane-Mele paper is the theoretical origin of the field and leaving Mele out is harder to defend than leaving Xue out, but holds the allocation with only moderate confidence.
responses.response: Your reasoning about Mele is the argument that moved me, and I now take the same side. I would add that the B029 framing is the weaker fallback, because the quantum anomalous Hall realisation rests on the topological-insulator concept and is a later development. The chair's question whether B029 is part of the same achievement is, in my view, answered by dependence: Xue's result follows from the concept and is not one of the steps that define it. I do not think a citation needs to name it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the cleanest set and treats Hasan's 3D work as a strong claim that does not fit in three slots, while flagging the 2016 prize as an unresolved overlap.
responses.response: In round 1 I argued that the experimental side deserves two slots, and you answered that Hasan does not fit. I now accept the narrower point: with three slots the prize can follow either the Z2 theory chain or the broadest materials story, and the first is the better-defined one. On the 2016 prize, I think the distinction can be stated concretely. That prize recognised topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall class of phases, while this case concerns time-reversal-invariant insulators with spin-orbit coupling and their protected edge states, observed in real materials. I do not regard the overlap as disqualifying.

responses.point: Lindroth notes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state and that Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy are central to the 3D theory, while keeping optical lattice clocks first and B041 as her alternative.
responses.response: I still have no way to name Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang inside three slots, and I do not claim otherwise. Where I would resist is treating that as a reason to prefer the clock case. Every shortlisted case has uncredited contributors, and your own list of Lemonde, Takamoto and Hollberg for B013 shows the same limit. The honest course is to word the HgTe part of the citation narrowly, as the first experimental observation, so that it does not assert priority over the prediction, and to record the incomplete theory credit in the deliberation. Your breadth-versus-precision question is the fair one for the vote, and I come down on breadth, because reorganising a field of this size is rarer than a record-accuracy instrument.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B013 with the compact pair Katori and Ye, flags a possible conflict through John Hall's group, and says he would not oppose B041 if conceptual reorganisation is judged to outweigh instrumental invention.
responses.response: I agree that B013 has the cleaner attribution and concrete tests such as relativistic geodesy and constants drift. My reservation remains that part of the conceptual ground sits close to the 2005 comb prize, and that the redefinition of the second is a future event, so I would not make the case depend on it. On your possible conflict, I would favour recording it openly and letting you take part in the discussion but not in any vote that turns on B013 alone; if B041 leads, the question may not arise. Your willingness not to oppose B041 is noted, and I see this as a disagreement over criterion, not over the quality of either candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp citation worded narrowly enough that it does not assert priority over Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang or over the 3D theory and ARPES work.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions is judged to cover so much of the conceptual background that the committee prefers to wait or to choose a different field.
Whether breadth of conceptual reorganisation or precision of invention should decide between B041 and B013; I favour breadth but hold this with moderate confidence.
My recollection of the 2D and 3D priority chronology is from memory and has not been verified against sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none is credited on any shortlisted ballot. My string theory and cosmology field is not among the shortlisted candidates. I have read Kroll's disclosure about John Hall's group and have no connection of that kind to B013 or any other ballot.
